{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
'''Cauchy's limit theorem''', named after the French mathematician [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]], describes a property of [[Limit of a sequence|converging sequences]]. It states that for a converging sequence the sequence of the [[arithmetic mean]]s of its first <math>n</math> members converges against the same limit as the original sequence, that is <math> (a_n)</math> with <math>a_n\to a</math> implies <math>(a_1+\cdots+a_n) / n \ \to a</math>.<ref name="Knopp">[[Konrad Knopp]]: ''Infinite Sequences and Series''. Dover, 1956, pp. 33-36</ref><ref name="Heuser">[[Harro Heuser]]: ''Lehrbuch der Analysis – Teil 1'', 17th edition, Vieweg + Teubner 2009, ISBN 9783834807779, pp. [https://books.google.com/books?id=CQ_wc67PkFQC&pg=PA177 176-179] (German)</ref> The theorem was found by Cauchy in 1821,<ref name="Knopp"/> subsequently a number of related and generalized results were published, in particular by [[Otto Stolz]] (1885) and [[Ernesto Cesàro]] (1888).<ref>J. Marshall Ash, Allan Berele, Stefan Catoiu: ''Plausible and Genuine Extensions of L’Hospital’s Rule''. In: ''Mathematics Magazine'', Vol. 85, No. 1, Februar 2012, pp. 52–60, [[doi:10.4169/math.mag.85.1.52]] ({{JSTOR|10.4169/math.mag.85.1.52}})</ref>

== Related results and generalizations ==
If the arithmetic means in Cauchy's limit theorem are replaced by [[weighted arithmetic mean]]s those converge as well. More precisely for sequence <math> (a_n)</math> with <math>a_n\to a </math> and a sequence of [[positive real numbers]] <math> (p_n)</math> with <math>\frac{1}{p_1+\cdots+p_n} \to 0</math> one has <math>\frac{p_1a_1+\cdots+p_na_n}{p_1+\cdots+p_n}\to a </math>.<ref name="Heuser"/><ref name="Knopp"/>

This result can be used to derive the [[Stolz–Cesàro theorem]], a more general result of which Cauchy's limit theorem is a [[special case]].<ref name="Heuser"/>

For the [[geometric mean]]s of a sequence a similar result exists. That is for a sequence <math>(a_n)</math> with <math>a_n>0</math> and <math>a_n\to a</math> one has <math>\sqrt[n]{a_1 \cdot a_2\cdot \cdots \cdot a_n} \ \to a</math>.<ref name="Heuser"/><ref name="Knopp"/>

The arithmetic means in Cauchy's limit theorem are also called [[Cesàro mean]]s. While Cauchy's limit theorem implies that for a convergent series its Cesàro means converge as well, the converse is not true. That is the Cesàro means may converge while the original sequence does not. Applying the latter fact on the partial sums of a [[Series (mathematics)|series]] allows for assigning real values to certain divergent series and leads to the concept of [[Cesàro summation]] and [[Summability theory|summable series]]. In this context Cauchy's limit theorem can be generalised into the [[Silverman–Toeplitz theorem]].<ref name="Knopp"/><ref>Johann Boos: ''Classical and Modern Methods in Summability''. Oxford University Press, 2000, ISBN 9780198501657, p. 9</ref>

== Proof ==
Let <math>\varepsilon>0</math> and <math>N \in \N</math> such that <math>|a_k - a| \leq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}</math> for all <math>k \geq N</math>. Due to <math>\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^N (a_k - a) = 0</math> there exists a <math>M \in \N</math> with <math>\left|\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^N (a_k - a)\right| \leq \frac{\varepsilon}{2}</math> for all <math>n \geq M</math> .

Now for all <math>n \geq \max(N,M)</math> the above yields:

:<math>\begin{align}
\left|\frac{1}{n} \left(\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\right) - a\right| 
  & = \left|\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n (a_k - a)\right| 
    = \left|\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^N (a_k - a) + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=N+1}^n (a_k - a)\right| \\ 
  & \leq \left|\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^N (a_k - a)\right| + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=N+1}^n |a_k - a| \leq \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{(n-N)\varepsilon}{2n} 
    \leq \varepsilon.
\end{align}</math><ref name="Heuser"/>
